title: What part of AI game development do you still prefer doing manually?
author: lollyadorable4
selftext:
As much as I read and study, I see that some people are comfortable letting AI handle most of the coding but want full control over game design and art direction. Others use it more for assets, debugging, tooling, or prototyping.

I’m curious where that line is now. What have you tried delegating to AI but ended up deciding you’d rather keep doing yourself?

comments.author: davesoft
comments.body: Browser testing. It only takes 1 browser test to 'pass' but doesn't work when deployed then the whole notion of browser testing gets turned off.

replies.author: lollyadorable4
replies.body: This is pretty much where I’d draw the line too. I feel like once you hand over the actual design decisions, it starts feeling less like your game. I’m curious tho, do you use AI at all when balancing or do you keep that completely manual too?

replies.author: Livid_Shallot5701
replies.body: Depends. When i have a skill and it has damage or buff it smth i balance myself from the beginning. If it's an interaction with a bunch of numbers like "the answer from the NPC depends on the interaction between these 8 social stats" I first let the ai draft some sort of matrix to connect them all and then tweak or redo it depending on the outcome. But it's always me ingame checking if it feels right

comments.author: _HoundOfJustice
comments.body: Art/assets is/are my things that i do not want to delegate to AI and as a professional artist i dont need to and i also have premade assets and libraries at disposal where needed and sufficient. Game design is generally something i want to have have under control as well with or without AI assistance. Prototyping is something i neither do fully on my own anymore (with art/assets its usually almost entirely manually if not entirely) , nor do i fully delegate it to AI.

replies.author: lollyadorable4
replies.body: thats probably closer to how I think about AI too than treating it like something that should make the whole game for you. keeping art and game design under your control while delegating implementation feels like a pretty solid balance 👌

comments.author: Fuzzzy420
comments.body: Playtest. Artstyle. And all the logic!

comments.author: oscar_unrealizex
comments.body:
Disclosure: I'm VP of Product and Marketing for UnrealizeX. 

That said! We clone reality, and do so without generative AI. Awesome models from as little as 3 photos, automatic retopology and PBR materials. And we have the Maths. So the meshes have gorgeous nooks and crannies, compared to the voxelized-with-a-texture-projected-back-on shrinkwrap look other systems produce. 

If you've ever done photoscanning, it's like that, but without the need for a huge dataset (which still produces a hideous polygon cloud in RC). But it creates a different workflow metric: how do you maximize datasets for 3D assets when you need a fraction of the input from workflows of a bygone era? So now I'm experimenting with city walks with a timelapse camera, and seeing how much data I can pull off the footage. Gonna go clone planet earth :D 

The other part of it I love: drawing and painting. We can one-shot a mesh off of concept art without generative AI, which is HUUGELY satisfying.  And it speaks to what IMO a perfect pipeline should be: ideas and creativity, poured out of an artist's hands, and then beep bop boop you've got a game ready 3D model. I love the dream that an artist makes some concept art, and there you go. All done. That's the whole 3D asset creation pipeline. 

[UnrealizeX — Cloning Reality from photos](https://unrealizex.com/)

comments.author: Time_Cat_5212
comments.body: The game systems and core design stuff.  I don't mind having LLMs write the code or generate assets, but I want to spec out how the core systems work in detail.  Leaving that up to inference usually results in flat, not particularly elegant, derivative systems.  The joy of a good game for me largely comes from having great, well designed mechanics.

replies.author: lollyadorable4
replies.body: YES, this distinction makes sm sense!! I don’t mind AI implementing a system, but I still want to be the one deciding exactly how that system should behave. Otherwise you end up with something technically functional but not necessarily fun kk

comments.author: SmoggySPECTEREGaming
comments.body: I like doing the actual world building and level design, so I can feel like I made that. I built it. I can still have creative freedom. But systems implementation is something I know less than the tip of the iceberg about. I am learning it, so I can get a fundamental understanding of what it's doing for me, but i am literally years away from being proficient at it.

replies.author: Brewgazer
replies.body: My favorite part is when things work when I thought surely it would take 5 more prompts trying to achieve one thing

replies.author: lollyadorable4
replies.body: that feeling when it works on the first try and you immediately get suspicious lol

comments.author: Witty-Tangerine3606
comments.body: I use FormFromLight an AI tool for 2d to 3d assets including world building and the core game mechanics I code myself, otherwise it gets messy and buggy spaghetti code

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: My ideal is to have LLMS help me with code so I can focus on hand drawn pixel art.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
All of the below, but not 100% manually, but assisted by AI, because it is great for making tooling, for learning and for bouncing ideas off of, and a lot more.

Also, what does "manual" even mean? I rather distinguish between automated and interactive. AI is involved everywhere. The real question is whether I have to sit in front of a PC and ping-communicate with AI, or use any other tool directly.

Art direction. All direction in fact.

Software rchitecture, sometimes all the way down to choosing code patterns when I know what works best.

Shader programming, but I've now figured out that AI can do it just fine if you give it the building blocks and know what you're doing. It's learning by doing, discovery and reuse of patterns, just like everything else. The idea that "AI can't do graphics programming" is perpetuated by 1. Vibe coders who can't do graphics programming and 2. Bitter graphics programmers "attempting" to vibe code graphics half-assed and dishonestly to make a point, rather than using their skills to find out what works.

QA and play testing, obviously. I'm working on strategies to automate some of it headless to detect regressions, but there is no way around actually playing the game. All you can do is find ways to do less of it without degrading quality.

Checking any higher level math done by AI, because AI gets math wrong the same way humans do.

Reading specs that are non-trivial and make significant architectural decisions, and making those decisions, of course. Sometimes I also "president Schwartzenegger" decisions and see how it goes. Failing with AI is cheap.

Also, I would NEVER leave composing music to AI. I'd rather not have music in my game at all. Music is a significant part of how a game feels. It either feels right, and the way I intend it to, or I leave that part to the players listening to their own music in the background.

comments.author: kultcher
comments.body:
All the high-level design elements, basically.

Game/mechanic design, game feel tuning, level design, UI/UX design, narrative flow. Art direction to a lesser extent, since I don't have an artist's eye, but I still will research and provide references for art style/influences when using AI art as placeholders.

comments.author: KnownPride
comments.body:
Game design, mechanic, testing and polishing.  I don't see current ai architecture ever able to build those. 

Even if Astra capabilities is 10x today it will still fail on all of those.

comments.author: OkPrice6335
comments.body: Lass KI nicht dein Ideengeber sein, so bleibt  menschlicher Geist im Produkt.
